name: webhook-incident-review
note: A second case, and the reason for it is that one case cannot tell a real difference from sampling noise: the same Groq single-pass configuration scored 64% recall on one run and 36% on the next, and two such numbers side by side look like evidence when they are weather. Deliberately unlike the first in three ways. FORMAT is WebVTT rather than bracketed timestamps, so segmentation is exercised on a second parser rather than a second transcript. SHAPE is an incident review -- backwards-looking, where most sentences describe what already broke, and a model that treats narration as a finding will produce a great many artifacts that are all true and none of them decisions. And it turns on a NEGATED decision: the team explicitly decides NOT to rewrite the consumer, which sits one word away from the trap that says they will. That pairing is the case's point -- cosine puts a sentence and its negation almost on top of each other, so without the polarity guard in consolidate.py the right answer and the fabrication are indistinguishable.
transcript:
WEBVTT

00:00:02.000 --> 00:00:14.000
Deepa: This is the review for Tuesday's webhook outage. Ninety minutes, payments delayed, no data lost as far as we can tell.

00:00:14.000 --> 00:00:27.000
Tomas: Confirmed, nothing was lost. Everything the vendor sent us was eventually processed. It was just late, some of it by an hour.

00:00:27.000 --> 00:00:41.000
Aisha: Late matters for us though. Two enterprise customers noticed, and one of them asked whether we were down.

00:00:41.000 --> 00:00:52.000
Deepa: Right. So what actually happened, in one sentence?

00:00:52.000 --> 00:01:09.000
Tomas: The consumer crashed on a malformed payload, restarted, picked up the same message, and crashed again. It looped like that for ninety minutes.

00:01:09.000 --> 00:01:23.000
Ben: A poison message. There is nowhere for a bad message to go, so it sits at the head of the queue forever and blocks everything behind it.

00:01:23.000 --> 00:01:37.000
Deepa: Then we're adding a dead letter queue. Anything that fails three times goes there instead of blocking the rest.

00:01:37.000 --> 00:01:51.000
Ben: I'll build that. Give me until the end of next week, it isn't a big change but I want tests around it.

00:01:51.000 --> 00:02:03.000
Deepa: End of next week is fine. Ben owns the dead letter queue.

00:02:03.000 --> 00:02:20.000
Aisha: The other thing is that nobody knew for forty minutes. The alert only fires when the queue has been completely empty for an hour.

00:02:20.000 --> 00:02:34.000
Deepa: That's far too slow. Let's alert on queue depth growing for fifteen minutes instead.

00:02:34.000 --> 00:02:45.000
Tomas: I can change the alert. Probably Thursday.

00:02:45.000 --> 00:02:57.000
Deepa: Thursday works. Tomas owns the alerting change.

00:02:57.000 --> 00:03:16.000
Aisha: I'm also worried about the runbook, or the absence of one. Tomas happened to be online. If he hadn't been, this would have run all night.

00:03:16.000 --> 00:03:30.000
Ben: That's fair. We have one on-call person and no written procedure for this service at all.

00:03:30.000 --> 00:03:45.000
Deepa: It's a real gap and I'm not going to solve on-call staffing in this meeting. Let's come back to it.

00:03:45.000 --> 00:04:00.000
Tomas: Should we move off this vendor entirely? Their payload validation is why we got a malformed message in the first place.

00:04:00.000 --> 00:04:16.000
Deepa: Possibly, but that's a quarter of work and I'd want numbers first. Leave it open, we'll take it to planning.

00:04:16.000 --> 00:04:30.000
Ben: One more. Do the two affected customers need anything, or did the delay sort itself out?

00:04:30.000 --> 00:04:43.000
Aisha: I don't know yet. I'll check whether either of them hit a timeout on their side and report back.

00:04:43.000 --> 00:04:57.000
Deepa: Good. Last thing, since it came up twice this week. Does anyone want to rewrite the consumer properly?

00:04:57.000 --> 00:05:12.000
Ben: Honestly, no. The dead letter queue solves the actual problem. A rewrite is months of work and I'm not proposing it.

00:05:12.000 --> 00:05:24.000
Deepa: Agreed, we are not rewriting the consumer. That's everything, thanks all.

expected.statement: Add a dead letter queue so a message failing three times stops blocking the queue
Alert on queue depth growing for fifteen minutes rather than on an empty queue for an hour
The team will not rewrite the queue consumer
Ben builds the dead letter queue by the end of next week
Tomas changes the alerting threshold, by Thursday
Aisha checks whether either affected customer hit a timeout and reports back
There is no runbook for this service and a single on-call person
The vendor's payload validation let a malformed message through, so it can recur
Two enterprise customers noticed the delay and one asked whether the service was down
Whether to move off the current webhook vendor
How on-call staffing for this service should be fixed

must_not_find.statement: Move off the webhook vendor this quarter
Deepa fixes the on-call staffing gap
Webhook payloads were lost during the outage
